title: When the riverbeds dry in eastern Chad, the walk for safe water gets longer
subtitle: Nearly 90 million people forced from home now live in countries highly exposed to climate hazards. Ahead of COP31, refugees are asking for a say in how money reaches the places where they live.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: A Sudanese woman who fled the fighting in El Fasher in June 2023 described a second kind of journey to the UN refugee agency. In Farchana, the settlement in eastern Chad where she found refuge, she has to walk farther for water as seasonal riverbeds dry up. Sometimes, she told the agency, a week passes without her finding water that is safe to drink.

Conflict explains why she left Sudan. The distance to safe water helps explain what it takes to stay in Chad. In a report released on 6 November ahead of the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Türkiye, UNHCR put a figure on the overlap: nearly 90 million forcibly displaced people, about three quarters of the global total, were living by mid-2026 in countries with high or extreme exposure to hazards such as drought, flooding and heat.

That estimate describes countries. It cannot tell a water engineer which pump runs dry first, how long a family queues or who in the household makes the trip. Nor is it a count of people displaced by climate change. Alongside the figures, the report draws on testimony from eight representatives of displaced communities. Their accounts explain consequences a national figure misses; they are too few to establish how common any one experience is.

UNHCR says fragile and conflict-affected countries receive about a tenth of global climate finance. That is the share going to a group of countries; the figure does not identify how much reaches refugees or their neighbours. At COP31 the agency is asking governments and lenders to include displaced people in national climate plans and to finance work that lasts beyond an emergency appeal.

In Farchana, the difference can be measured in hours. An emergency delivery can supply water today. Keeping water within reach through a dry season also takes storage, a reliable source and someone with the means to maintain it. The women who make the journey can tell planners when a source stops being useful, even if it still appears on a map.

In the Rohingya camps of Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh, women already do some of the work such plans depend on. The International Organization for Migration says women volunteers visit households to explain cyclone warnings and how to prepare for the monsoon. Three women it identified as Arefa, Tahera and Razia also trained to operate mobile firefighting units built for the camps’ narrow paths. For Tahera, driving one gave her a way to serve neighbours and a chance to learn a skill she had long wanted.

The same funding question follows families home. More than two thirds of refugees who returned to their countries in the first half of 2026 went back to countries highly vulnerable to climate hazards, UNHCR found. That does not mean those returns failed. It does mean a count of people who crossed a border tells governments little about whether they will be able to stay.
For the woman in Farchana, the most telling measure of a climate investment would be close to home: when the riverbed dries again, how far will she have to go for water her family can drink?
